subtitle: When learned meanings differ, how do you communicate well? Choose a suitable approach while staying truthful and authentic, and pay close attention to how the other person actually responds.
scope: For staff across DHS. CQ® Action is explored through David Livermore, Leading with Cultural Intelligence (3rd ed., HarperCollins Leadership, 2024, chapter 7) and original practice, not a proprietary assessment or prescription for a community. Personal and practice learning can remain private and unrecorded. A changed communication approach does not alter actual criteria, permission or authority. Native American- and Tribal-specific matters are referred to the appropriate office within ADSA. CQ® is a registered trademark of Cultural Intelligence Center, LLC. These applications are not affiliated with Cultural Intelligence Center, LLC, or with David Livermore. They do not use the licensed CQ scale or show CQ scores.
introTranscript: Understanding another meaning can open a choice about how you respond. In this course, Ellis and Parker disagree about a book. One associates direct challenge with taking ideas seriously; the other associates acknowledging an idea before challenging it with taking the person seriously. You will explore suitable words, pauses and ways of checking a response without pretending to agree or copying a cultural performance. The practice path does not require a personal story, real interaction or work result.

lessons.title: Connect understanding with a suitable response
objectives: Identify a learned meaning behind two practice disagreement styles.
Distinguish understanding, behavioral adjustment and an actual effect.
takeaways: Action concerns a response, not only knowing another meaning.
A suitable adjustment can preserve an honest opinion.
An attempted action and its effect are different claims.
lessons.statement: Let understanding inform a truthful behavioral choice.

image.caption: Colleagues share information and consider a decision together.

intro.heading: Connect understanding with a suitable response
intro.body:
In Leading with Cultural Intelligence (3rd ed., 2024, chapter 7), David Livermore describes CQ Action as being yourself while working out which behaviors must change to reach the goal (about pp. 151-52). It has three parts: speech acts, or the words you use; verbal, such as speed and volume; and nonverbal, such as eye contact and gesture. The chapter’s title carries his caution: adapt, but not too much. The original exercises here examine possible communication choices; they do not administer an assessment or supply a required style for a demographic group.

Ellis and Parker discuss a book they both chose to read. Ellis learned that directly challenging an argument can show that it deserves serious attention. Parker volunteers a different learned meaning: first acknowledging what is understood can show regard for the person before a challenge. Each account concerns respect, but the order and expression differ.

Ellis understands why an immediate challenge can sound dismissive to Parker. Action adds a further choice: Ellis could briefly acknowledge the point before offering the same honest disagreement. The adjustment need not weaken the opinion or declare Parker’s approach universally best. It connects the actual meaning to a possible response.

Whether the reply helps is a separate question. The practice exercise can develop personal understanding without a real conversation. The official IDC is a distinct five-orientation framework; ordinary adjustment is not automatically its Adaptation, which involves culturally informed perspective and behavior. Neither framework permits an individual result to be inferred from this exchange.

flashcards.back: Adapting behavior as needed across cultural backgrounds, explored here through original communication choices.
A change in expression that remains truthful and fits the person’s real purpose and limits.
A specific action such as acknowledging a point, changing the order of a reply or explaining a pause.
More than one possible way to express a purpose, rather than a fixed script for a group.
Whether the action fits this actual situation and response; good intention alone does not establish it.
What actually followed from an action, requiring its own information rather than assumed from effort.

items.title: The contrast gives the action a reason
items.body: Ellis is not simply adding pleasant words. Acknowledgment addresses Parker’s volunteered meaning of being taken seriously as a person. The reason matters because it connects the choice to understanding, rather than decorating an unchanged dismissal with a generic polite phrase.

items.title: The view can remain honest
items.body: Ellis can acknowledge the argument and still disagree with its conclusion. A suitable adjustment concerns how the reply is offered, not a requirement to surrender a belief. Distinguishing expression from agreement avoids making cultural learning a demand for conformity.

items.title: The action does not settle the effect
items.body: A considerate attempt may still miss the point or be unwelcome. Parker’s actual response would matter if a real exchange occurred. In the example, examine the reasoning and leave the relationship effect open rather than use effort as proof of success.

tabs.label: Understand without choosing a response
tabs.body: Ellis may accurately explain Parker’s meaning while continuing the same immediate dismissal. Knowledge can be valuable, but it is not the same as a changed action. Consider a specific option if an interaction is intended, while recognizing that private understanding remains worthwhile on its own.

tabs.label: Pretend to agree
tabs.body: Saying the argument is convincing when Ellis does not believe it may produce apparent harmony at the cost of truth. Parker’s meaning does not require false agreement. Acknowledging what was heard can preserve regard while leaving the genuine difference visible.

tabs.label: Choose a truthful acknowledgment
tabs.body: Ellis can state the point understood and then explain the disagreement. This connects a behavioral choice to the volunteered meaning without promising acceptance. It leaves Parker able to correct the understanding and both people able to retain their views.

check.question: Which response best illustrates the course’s use of CQ Action?

wrong: Ellis pretends to agree to prove cultural skill.
Understanding the meaning proves the relationship improved.
Parker’s preference establishes an individual IDC orientation.
check.feedbackCorrect: The response connects meaning and behavior while keeping honesty, effect evidence and assessment boundaries distinct.
check.feedbackIncorrect: False agreement is not required. Understanding alone does not establish an effect. A preference cannot establish an IDC orientation. Choose an authentic action for the actual meaning and retain uncertainty about what follows.

Ellis can acknowledge the point before disagreeing.

intro.heading: Change the expression without changing the truth
intro.body:
Ellis wants to disagree with the book’s conclusion. A direct response such as “That argument misses the point” reflects the value Ellis attaches to rigorous challenge. Parker hears it as a dismissal of the effort to explain. The volunteered meanings create a reason to consider a different sequence, not a rule banning disagreement.

Ellis could say, “I understand that you read the ending as a choice about responsibility. I read it differently because the earlier action matters to me.” The reply identifies what was understood and provides a reason for the disagreement. Parker can correct the interpretation. It does not announce that the two readings are equally convincing or that the discussion has reached agreement.

The choice should match the actual purpose. If Ellis has not understood the point, a clarification is more truthful than a polished acknowledgment invented to sound considerate. If the issue requires a definite answer, indirect reassurance that conceals the answer is not a suitable substitute. Clear language and cultural consideration can work together.

Use the invented passage and replies for private practice. You can reflect on a familiar association between honesty and a particular speaking order without sharing a personal conflict. The learning may broaden your options while you retain the views and expressions you actually value.

Livermore still admits his mistakes, and changes how, when and where he does it (chapter 1, about pp. 20-22). He shows that requests, apologies and praise carry different meanings in different settings (chapter 7, about pp. 152-56). In these applications, rights and safety are values that stay, and an agency’s apology does not replace changing the practice.

items.title: Acknowledgment is a claim about understanding
items.body: The phrase should identify a point Ellis genuinely heard. It does not need to endorse the conclusion. A specific acknowledgment can make regard visible while allowing correction, whereas empty praise may obscure whether the argument was understood at all.

items.title: A different sequence need not soften the reason
items.body: Ellis can retain a clear disagreement after identifying the understood point. The sequence responds to Parker’s meaning of regard, while the reason keeps the intellectual difference available for discussion. Neither person has to choose between being truthful and being taken seriously.

items.title: Clarity matters when the answer is definite
items.body: In a real task, a required answer should not disappear behind reassurance. Consider a suitable expression that states the actual position and reason within the relevant role. Cultural consideration does not authorize a misleading promise or a concealed decision.

tabs.label: Empty praise before dismissal
tabs.body: Calling the argument brilliant and then dismissing it without engagement may sound polished while saying little that is true. The phrase should have a basis. Acknowledgment is useful when it reflects actual understanding, not when it becomes a routine mask for a preselected response.

tabs.label: Truth used to justify any expression
tabs.body: Ellis may argue that a sincere disagreement makes every delivery equally suitable. Sincerity does not establish how the reply fits the actual exchange. Retain the truth and examine the expression, rather than treating a familiar style as the only possible honest one.

tabs.label: Specific understanding and a clear reason
tabs.body: Identify the point as understood, invite correction if needed and explain the disagreement. This creates another authentic option rather than a cultural performance. The difference remains visible, and the next response can add information instead of being forced into agreement.

check.question: Which reply distinguishes acknowledgment from agreement?
check.correct: State the point genuinely understood and explain the actual disagreement, leaving room for correction.
wrong: Praise the view falsely before dismissing it.
Hide the disagreement to make the exchange appear successful.
Treat sincere intention as proof that any delivery is suitable.
check.feedbackCorrect: The reply preserves the truth while providing a meaningful alternative expression.
check.feedbackIncorrect: False praise misrepresents understanding. Hiding disagreement substitutes appearance for an honest exchange. Sincere intention does not establish suitability. Identify what is genuinely understood and express the actual difference with a reason.

items.text: I understand your reading as a question about responsibility.
I disagree because the earlier action matters to my reading.
Have I understood the point you meant?
Does the task require a definite answer rather than reassurance?
Praise a view you do not actually consider convincing.
Hide the difference to report apparent agreement.

lessons.statement: Clarify the relevant meaning rather than diagnose the signal.

intro.heading: Use pauses and other signals with context
intro.body:
During the practice discussion, Parker pauses before responding to a challenge. Parker volunteers that a short pause can show consideration: the reply should reflect the idea rather than react immediately. Ellis associates a quick response with engagement and worries that silence means the discussion is unwelcome. The different meanings concern how attention is expressed, not which person thinks better.

Parker could briefly say, “I am considering the point before I reply.” That makes the relevant purpose available without requiring a performance of a presumed cultural style. Ellis can allow room for the response instead of filling the silence with another challenge. These are possible actions for this account, not instructions for how every person should use pauses.

The signal still needs context. If no meaning is volunteered, a pause might remain uncertain. Do not read it as consent, discomfort, lack of understanding or a formal cultural result. A relevant check or time to respond can be appropriate; repeated demands for an explanation can become pressure.

You can practice silently through the example. There is no required gaze pattern, gesture, tone or pause length to demonstrate. A learner may recognize a habitual interpretation of silence as a meaningful private insight even when no actual behavioral change follows.

Livermore says silence can mean many things and asks leaders to make room for reflection and for lively debate (chapter 7, about p. 160). He also tells of a hiring manager who doubted a candidate over eye contact, and he gives only a cultural reading of it (about pp. 159-60). These applications add disability: autism, blindness, Deaf communication and anxiety can all play a part. Treat a signal as a question, and test what the work requires.

lessons.keyStatement: Clarify the relevant meaning rather than diagnose the signal.

items.title: The contrast concerns meanings of attention
items.body: Quick engagement and considered response can both signal attention in the volunteered accounts. The same visible pause may therefore be interpreted differently. Understanding the contrast prevents the learner from treating speed as a reliable measure of interest or ability.

items.title: A short explanation can support an authentic action
items.body: Parker’s statement identifies the purpose of the pause in this exchange. It need not imitate another person’s voice or reproduce a community gesture. The behavior responds to the actual misunderstanding while allowing Parker’s own way of thinking and speaking to remain intact.

items.title: Unexplained signals can remain uncertain
items.body: A pause without an account does not settle agreement or emotion. Notice what is available and what is not. A proportionate clarification can help, but another person need not provide a personal history to satisfy curiosity about every movement or silence.

tabs.label: Diagnose the pause
tabs.body: Calling silence inability, refusal or consent converts a signal into a finding the exchange does not support. It can also lead to an inaccurate answer being assigned to the person. Retain uncertainty and use the actual account or a proportionate clarification.

tabs.label: Copy a prescribed performance
tabs.body: A fixed pause length or gaze rule for a presumed group replaces the individual exchange with a script. It may be uncomfortable or misleading. Choose an authentic behavior that serves the purpose rather than perform a cultural identity or treat one signal as universally respectful.

tabs.label: Make the relevant purpose available
tabs.body: Parker can explain the pause as consideration in this account, and Ellis can leave room for the response. That adjustment connects behavior and meaning. It does not promise that every pause has the same purpose or make the person responsible for explaining all nonverbal conduct.

check.question: Which conclusion fits the practice pause?
check.correct: Parker’s volunteered meaning can guide a suitable response here; an unexplained pause in another setting remains uncertain.
wrong: A fixed cultural gaze rule must be copied to show respect.
check.feedbackCorrect: The conclusion uses the actual account without turning it into a universal signal or performance rule.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A pause does not always mean agreement. Speed cannot establish intercultural capability. A prescribed gaze performance is not required. Use the volunteered meaning for this exchange and retain uncertainty where the actual account is absent.

items.text: Parker says the pause allows consideration before replying.
Ellis can leave room for the actual response.
An unexplained pause may have several meanings.
A declined explanation does not establish a motive.
Every silence is consent.

intro.heading: Build options without performing another identity
intro.body:
Ellis now has several possible responses. A clarification can be useful when the argument is unclear. A specific acknowledgment followed by a reasoned disagreement can be useful when the point is understood. A request to pause the discussion can be useful when the exchange needs time. These options serve different purposes; they are not a menu of styles assigned to groups.

Parker’s volunteered meanings help Ellis understand why acknowledgment and time can matter. They do not require Ellis to copy Parker’s accent, gestures, personal identity or every preference. A communication repertoire expands how a real purpose can be expressed while preserving the person’s own truthful voice.

Suitability also includes choice. Parker may decline to continue discussing the book, and Ellis may retain a different view. A changed expression should not become a technique for securing agreement or extracting an explanation. The aim is a more informed interaction, not control over the other person’s response.

Privately compare the options in the example and choose a reason for one. You may also simply recognize that your familiar style is not the only honest one. No actual conversation, imitation exercise or entered personal account is needed.

Livermore warns that heavy copying reads as insincere (chapter 7, about pp. 166-67). He offers questions on whether to adapt, which in our words are: how firm are the rules here, would adapting compromise the organization or you, what best reaches the goal, and would keeping the difference make the group stronger (about pp. 167-69)? When you cannot adapt, say what you can offer (about p. 168). In public service, legal duties and rights are lines that do not move, and these questions cannot weigh them away.

lessons.keyStatement: Expand your options while remaining yourself.

items.title: Match the option to the purpose
items.body: If Ellis is uncertain about the argument, a clarification is more suitable than pretending to understand it. If the point is clear, a reasoned disagreement may follow acknowledgment. Expanding options makes these distinctions available rather than adding phrases without regard to the task.

items.title: A repertoire is not a cultural costume
items.body: Copying an accent or gesture can misrepresent the person and distract from the meaning. The useful choice concerns a real communication purpose. Ellis can change the sequence of a reply in Ellis’s own voice instead of imitating Parker’s identity.

items.title: A different answer remains possible
items.body: An informed expression cannot guarantee agreement or continued participation. Respect a declined exchange and retain the actual difference. A communication option should not be offered as a way to make another person responsible for confirming the learner’s flexibility.

tabs.label: Use one formula in every exchange
tabs.body: A rehearsed acknowledgment can become empty when the point was not understood or the task needs a direct answer. A repertoire should help distinguish purposes. Choose the response for this account rather than apply a polished formula merely because it worked in the example.

tabs.label: Imitate to secure acceptance
tabs.body: Copying a perceived cultural performance may make the reply less truthful or appropriate. It also treats acceptance as the goal regardless of the other person’s choice. Respond in your own voice to the actual meaning rather than reproduce a presumed identity.

tabs.label: Choose an authentic option with a reason
tabs.body: Ellis can explain why a clarification, acknowledgment or pause fits this moment. The response remains genuine and open to correction. That reasoning makes flexibility purposeful while leaving Parker free to disagree or end the exchange.

check.question: Which statement best describes a useful repertoire?
check.correct: Several authentic options can serve different purposes without predicting a group or controlling another person’s response.
wrong: One polished phrase should be used regardless of understanding.
Copying an accent proves cultural respect.
The option is successful only if the other person agrees.
check.feedbackCorrect: A repertoire expands suitable expression without reducing a person to a performance or required outcome.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A phrase needs an actual purpose and basis. Accent imitation does not prove respect. Another person’s agreement is not guaranteed or owed. Choose a truthful option for the situation and retain the other person’s choice.

lessons.statement: Adjust the expression and preserve the real standard.

image.caption: Colleagues share information and consider a decision together.

intro.heading: Adapt feedback while retaining actual work criteria
intro.body:
In a separate practice DHS feedback exchange, Rowan sees direct correction as respecting a colleague’s ability to address a problem. Sam volunteers that first stating the contribution understood can show that a correction considers the work rather than dismisses the person. The supervisor can understand both meanings without treating either preference as a measure of performance.

A possible reply names the actual contribution, describes the specific task issue and explains the applicable criterion. This changes the sequence of expression without hiding the concern or inventing praise. The feedback should have a basis in the actual work and the assigned process, not a presumed cultural trait.

The learning does not authorize changing hiring or performance criteria, promising a personnel result or inferring an employee’s CQ® or IDC result. Staff and supervisors retain actual role and review requirements. Consultant guidance can help the reasoning while staff remain responsible for their work.

If a protected-class allegation arises, the actual reporting duty remains distinct. Under MMB Policy 1436, managers and supervisors immediately report such allegations or incidents to HR or the agency affirmative action officer and follow agency procedures. A more considerate feedback conversation must not postpone that step or become an improvised investigation outside assigned authority.

Livermore observes that adapting is expected more of women, gay people and Black people (chapter 7, about pp. 165-66). He names the imbalance and leaves it there. These applications add a rule of their own: the institution and those with more power adapt first, and the people served adapt least. He also says willingness to change processes, policies and timelines counts for more than etiquette (about p. 168).

lessons.keyStatement: Adjust the expression and preserve the real standard.

items.title: The contribution should be real
items.body: A supervisor can identify a specific contribution rather than manufacture praise to make a correction acceptable. The acknowledgment then has a basis and can clarify which part of the work is being discussed. Honest regard and a clear concern can be expressed together.

items.title: The criterion remains visible
items.body: A suitable sequence can change how feedback is received without altering what the actual task requires. State the issue and criterion plainly. Do not turn a cultural explanation into an undocumented exception or make a communication preference evidence that an employee lacks capability.

items.title: Keep a formal concern in its actual process
items.body: A feedback conversation can be useful while a separate allegation requires immediate reporting. The actions answer different questions. Preserve the assigned complaint and investigation procedures rather than making the employee’s acceptance of a revised style a gate to the required response.

tabs.label: Change the criterion to avoid discomfort
tabs.body: A supervisor might remove the task concern so the exchange appears agreeable. That can hide the actual standard and exceed authority. A considerate expression should clarify the work issue, not substitute an undocumented exception or misleading account of performance.

tabs.label: Judge capability from the preferred style
tabs.body: Calling Sam unable to receive feedback because acknowledgment matters treats a volunteered meaning as a deficit. The actual work needs its own evidence and criteria. Explore the communication preference without converting it into a personnel or assessment result.

tabs.label: Use clear, evidenced feedback
tabs.body: Identify a real contribution, state the task issue and criterion and invite relevant clarification through the assigned process. This connects the expression to the actual meaning while preserving responsibility. Any separate protected-class concern retains its required route and does not wait for the conversation to succeed.

check.question: Which approach preserves cultural consideration and actual responsibility?
check.correct: Adjust the feedback expression while retaining real task evidence, criteria, authority and required reporting.
wrong: Change the standard privately to guarantee comfort.
Infer capability from a preference for acknowledgment.
Wait for the revised conversation to succeed before a required manager report.
check.feedbackCorrect: Communication flexibility can coexist with clear standards and formal responsibilities.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A style adjustment does not authorize a private standards change. Preference does not establish capability. A required immediate report cannot wait for a conversation to succeed. Use actual work evidence and the assigned process alongside a suitable expression.

Explain the task concern in clear language.
Use actual criteria and assigned review authority.
A manager immediately reports a protected-class allegation through the proper route.
A preference establishes a personnel result.
A revised style replaces required reporting.

intro.heading: Review the action and keep learning open
intro.body:
Ellis understood another meaning of regard, considered a different sequence and remained truthful about the disagreement. Parker’s volunteered account helped explain a pause. These details support an account of learning and possible action in the example. They do not show what occurred in a real relationship or establish a commercial assessment result.

An action’s effect needs its own information. If a reply is actually used, relevant feedback can help assess whether the intended message was understood. A polite ending or no feedback does not prove that all concerns were resolved. Missing information also does not prove failure; keep the effect open rather than invent an answer.

The learner may gain a broader understanding of honesty or regard without conducting an interaction. That private growth is worthwhile. It can remain unrecorded and need not be converted into a work metric. An honest difference may remain after a considerate response.

Further practice can use another example or an appropriate actual context. Carry forward the reasoning about meaning and purpose rather than a fixed script of words or gestures. If actual work is undertaken, retain its proper evidence, authority and required processes.

Livermore says asking whether people follow does not check anything, so build in questions or activities that show what landed (chapter 7, about p. 158). He also suggests talking an interaction through with someone afterward (about p. 172).

items.title: Describe the attempt precisely
items.body: If Ellis used an acknowledgment, that is the action to name. Whether Parker felt understood is another claim. Precise description protects the value of a real attempt without making it prove an outcome or personal status that the available information cannot establish.

items.title: Do not make missing feedback a verdict
items.body: Silence at the end may leave the effect unclear. It neither certifies success nor establishes failure. Use relevant information when appropriately available and acknowledge what remains unknown instead of assigning the other person a reaction for the purpose of completing the review.

items.title: Carry understanding rather than a formula
items.body: Another person may attach a different meaning to direct challenge or a pause. The useful practice is to connect an authentic response to the actual account. Retaining a private insight can be sufficient; more encounters are not required to validate the learning.

tabs.label: Report effort as guaranteed success
tabs.body: A thoughtful reply can still be misunderstood or unsuitable. Reporting it as guaranteed success hides the effect question. Name the actual behavior and use relevant information for any wider claim rather than assume that intent and effort establish the other person’s experience.

tabs.label: Require a work metric for personal growth
tabs.body: Recognizing another possible meaning of honesty can matter without an operational measure. An actual work-effect claim needs evidence, but that separate requirement does not invalidate private understanding. The practice path can conclude without disclosure, a real interaction or a submitted work product.

tabs.label: Recognize and reconsider
tabs.body: Retain the supported meaning, action and uncertainty, then choose another inquiry if useful. This values learning without awarding a score or imposing a cultural formula. An actual duty remains in its proper process if a real situation is used.

check.question: Which review best matches the practice learning?
check.correct: Recognize the supported insight and possible action, retain unknown effects and choose further inquiry without a score or required work result.
wrong: A thoughtful attempt guarantees that the person felt respected.
Missing feedback proves no concerns remain.
Private understanding is invalid unless a work measure changes.
check.feedbackCorrect: The review values the actual gain while keeping effects and operational claims separate.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A thoughtful attempt cannot guarantee another person’s experience. Missing feedback is not reassurance. Private understanding does not need a work measure to matter. Recognize what is supported and keep unknown effects open.

lessons.transfer: Privately retain an insight or question from the example. No entered account, personal performance, actual interaction or work metric is required.

move.control: You can value a meaningful action choice without overstating its effect.
move.failure: Review becomes a result guarantee or demand for operational proof.
move.next: Recognize the supported gain and keep context and evidence visible.

jobAid.subtitle: Choose an authentic action for an actual meaning and review what follows honestly.
remember: CQ Action concerns behavior; this course does not administer a CQ or IDI assessment or prescribe a community performance.
A change in expression can preserve an honest opinion and actual task criteria.
Private practice understanding can matter without an entered story, real interaction or work result.

sections.heading: Choose the response
items: Identify the purpose and the volunteered or practice meaning relevant to it.
Consider a clarification, genuine acknowledgment, clear disagreement or explained pause as appropriate to the actual account.
Keep the expression truthful; do not imitate an identity, promise agreement or diagnose a signal.
Retain the other person’s choice to correct, disagree or decline the exchange.

sections.heading: Apply and review
items: Keep actual work evidence, criteria, permission and authority in their proper process.
Preserve required Policy 1436 immediate manager reporting; a revised style does not replace or delay it.
Describe understanding and an attempted action separately from an effect, keeping missing information unknown.
Carry the reasoning into another context rather than a fixed cultural formula, and choose further practice only if useful.

sources.title: Cultural Intelligence Center: What is cultural intelligence?
sources.note: Public CQ Action capability within the four-capability framework. Original communication options are learning examples, not a proprietary assessment, community script or guarantee.

sources.title: David Livermore, Leading with Cultural Intelligence: The Real Secret to Success, 3rd ed. (HarperCollins Leadership, 2024)
sources.note: Action and its three parts, and when to adapt (chapter 2, about p. 31; chapter 7, about pp. 151-69), paraphrased from the book. Livermore is a founder of the Cultural Intelligence Center. His question list is restated in our words, and his style table and distance figures are not used. No personal score is adopted.

sources.title: Council of Europe: Developing intercultural competence through education
sources.note: Supports interpreting meanings, verbal and nonverbal communication and thoughtful action. The course examples do not reproduce source exercises or impose Minnesota rules.

sources.title: IDI: Intercultural Development Continuum
sources.note: The distinct official five-orientation continuum and culturally informed perspective-and-behavior boundary for Adaptation. Ordinary adjustment, a preference or a course response does not establish an individual orientation.

sources.title: DHS Equity Policy
sources.note: Actual equity responsibilities remain relevant to daily practice. Communication flexibility does not replace required analysis, authorize a criteria change or establish an equitable personnel result.

sources.title: MMB Policy 1436: Harassment and discrimination prohibited
sources.note: Actual immediate manager and supervisor reporting to HR or the affirmative action officer and assigned agency procedures. A changed expression does not replace or delay the required response.
